8.0.s.en: 1. Wisdom is a helper for all

8.0.0.en: 1 She reaches from one end to the other with strength, and orders all things with gentleness.

8.0.1.en: She extends with power from the farthest end of the world to its farthest end, and orders all things well. [1]

8.0.2.en: The divine wisdom is the source of the order of the world, for He is a God of order and not of confusion (1 Cor 14:33), yet this order is offered for the edification of man. St. Augustine often used this phrase to affirm the care of God's wisdom wherever we may be, and His constant ordering of things for our sake.

8.0.3.en: * The Word of God, who is also the Son of God, co-eternal with the Father, the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor 1:24). He extends by His might in a harmony that orders all things, from the greatest in intelligence to the least of material creation, creation visible and hidden, without being limited or divided or enlarged, but is present in His entirety without having any dimensions.

8.0.4.en: * What then, brethren? "All things were made by him." By this we have understood that all creation was made through the Son. The Father made it by His Word; God made it by His power and wisdom. Can we say that when He created things "all things were made by him," but that now the Father does not do all things through Him? God forbid! Let such thoughts be driven far from the hearts of believers. Let them be driven far from the thoughts of the devout and the understanding of the religious! It cannot be that the Father created through Him but did not order creation through Him. God forbid that He should not order what He brought into being, those things that were created through Him and received their existence through Him! See from the testimony of Holy Scripture itself that not only were all things created through Him, if we quote from the Gospel "All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made," but that all the things that were made are also ordered and arranged through Him. You know that Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God; know also what has been said of wisdom: "She extends from one end to the other with strength, and orders (with might) all things well" (Wis 8:1). So let us not doubt that all things are ordered through Him by whom all things were made. Thus the Father does nothing without the Son, nor the Son without the Father.

8.0.5.en: St. Augustine. Some ask: If the Son was sent into the world, was He not in the world before this mission was accomplished? He was in the world by the power of His divinity, but His mission concerns His incarnation, that He might accomplish salvation by the Cross and the Resurrection.

8.0.6.en: * He came into the world, and He was in the world. So He was sent to where He already was. Note also what was written through the prophet: "Do not I fill heaven and earth? saith the LORD" (Jer 23:24)... He who says, "I fill heaven and earth," was in every place... If it is said that this concerns the Father, how could the Father exist without His Word and without His wisdom, which "reaches with power from one end of the world to the other, and orders all things sweetly" (Wis 8:1)?

8.0.7.en: St. Augustine. He is the author of order and of providence, through which we touch not only the greatness of His power but also the sweetness of His love, which works for our sake in this ordering of the universe. He desires to keep the order working for our sake, yet He may break one of the natural laws if that is for our edification. In His love He does this, not to display His miracles, signs and wonders, but to proclaim His love and tenderness and the sweetness of His ordering of all things for our sake.

8.0.8.en: St. Augustine often used this phrase to affirm the presence of God in every place, and His continual care and providence in every place.

8.0.9.en: The appearing of God to Moses on Mount Sinai, where there was fire and smoke (Ex 19:18-19), does not mean that God, whether the Holy Trinity or one of the hypostases, was limited in His presence to one particular place and not another. It was so that Moses might be able to see God that He appeared thus in a particular place and in a manner in which He could be seen. But He is present in the whole world.

8.0.10.en: We do not wonder when we read: "And mount Sinai was altogether on a smoke, because the LORD descended upon it in fire" (Ex 19:18). And also: "And they saw the God of Israel: and there was under his feet as it were a paved work of a sapphire stone" (Ex 24:10).

8.0.11.en: Also in God's saying to Moses, "Thou shalt see my back parts: but my face shall not be seen" (Ex 33:23), and when the Apostle Paul says that we shall see Him face to face (1 Cor 13:12), and the saying of the Apostle John: "but we know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is" (1 Jn 3:2). These expressions and the like do not mean that God has members, or can be divided, or exists in one place and not in another, but it is a condescension on His part so that we may enjoy Him and be able to see Him and speak with Him.

8.0.12.en: Again, when St. Augustine spoke of the snares that Satan sets for men, he said that the wisdom of God extends over all the world and orders all things sweetly, so that it turns the evils and plots of the devil into the benefit and glory of man.

8.1.0.en: 2 I loved her and sought her out from my youth, and desired to take her for my bride, and I became a lover of her beauty. 3 For in her noble birth there is glory, because she lives with God, and the Lord of all has loved her, and she is the one whom I loved and sought from my youth, and strove to take her for my bride, and became a lover of her beauty. [2]

8.1.1.en: Wisdom is not acquired by human effort alone, but is given as a gift of God.

8.1.2.en: * From the will springs wisdom, with which the wise man enters into marriage, saying: "I sought to take her for my bride" (Wis 8:2). This will, which was formerly weak and lukewarm with the fever of diverse desires, rose up afterward, through the ministry of the Apostles, strong for the service of Christ.

8.1.3.en: St. Ambrose. * It is Solomon who says that he longs to make wisdom his bride (Wis 8:2). And in another place he says again of wisdom: "Love her, and she will embrace you; embrace her, and she will keep you" (cf. Prov 4:6, 8). Let us also take her to ourselves as a wife! Let us hold her in our arms, and not let her leave our embrace, nor let her flee from our arms. If this bride is always in our bosom, we shall beget children from her (that is, the fruit of the Spirit and not of the flesh).

8.1.4.en: St. Jerome. Origen sees that Sarah points to wisdom, so that Abraham, the righteous man of God, clung to her as his princess bride, to whom he listens in all that she says.

8.1.5.en: * I believe that "Sarah," which means "a ruling princess," represents arete, which is the virtue of the soul. This virtue, then, accompanies the wise and faithful man and clings to him, exactly as the wise man said of wisdom: "I desired to take her to me for a wife" (Wis 8:2). For this reason the Lord said to Abraham: "In all that Sarah hath said unto thee, hearken unto her voice" (Gen 21:12). This saying, however, does not suit bodily marriage, for it is known that the word was declared from heaven to the woman: [Your refuge shall be to him, and he shall rule over you] (cf. Gen 3:16). If the husband is said to be the lord of his wife, how is it said to Abraham, "In all that Sarah hath said unto thee, hearken unto her voice"? But if he is married to virtue, then in all that she counsels him, let him listen to her.

8.1.6.en: * In fact, God distinguishes the progress of the saints by likening it to marriage. You too, if you wish, can become a husband of this kind. For example, if you practice hospitality, you will seem to have taken this virtue as a wife. If you add to that compassion for the poor, you have a second wife. But if you also acquire patience and gentleness and the other virtues, you will seem to have as many wives as the virtues you have acquired.

8.2.0.en: Origen. She glorifies her noble origin by her sharing in the life of God, and the Lord of all has loved her. [3]

8.2.1.en: What is the noble origin of wisdom, if not that she is the Second Divine Hypostasis, begotten of the Father from eternity, Light from Light, true God from true God, one with Him in the same essence?

8.2.2.en: This is the wisdom of God who became incarnate in order to reflect upon us dignity and honor from His noble origin, for being the only-begotten Son He gave us sonship to the Father in the waters of Baptism by His Holy Spirit, so that we have come to glory in this sonship.

8.2.3.en: As for wisdom's sharing in the life of the Father, the Lord Christ Himself says to the Father: "And all mine are thine, and thine are mine" (Jn 17:9).

8.2.4.en: By His incarnation He offered us the life of communion with God, by our union with the Father in the Holy Spirit through the merit of the shed blood of the Lord Christ. We have gained the right to enjoy heavenly and divine things as divine gifts that we receive through our reconciliation with the Father by the Cross.

8.2.5.en: As for the love of the Lord of all for wisdom, the Lord Christ says: "for thou lovedst me before the foundation of the world" (Jn 17:24); and He came to carry us to His Father so that we might enjoy His love. "That the love wherewith thou hast loved me may be in them, and I in them" (Jn 17:26).

8.2.6.en: It is as though the wise man asks us to acquire the wisdom of God, so that we may acquire the following:

8.2.7.en: A. The reflection of His noble origin upon us, so that He raises us from the dunghill to sit with the nobles of the nobles of His people.

8.2.8.en: B. Enjoyment of fellowship with God, or fellowship in the divine nature, so that we walk in the truth as children of God.

8.2.9.en: C. We carry wisdom, so that we truly become the object of God's surpassing love, and the possibility of loving God, the Lord of all, becomes ours.

8.3.s.en: 3. Wisdom is the giver of riches

8.3.0.en: 4 For she is the initiate in the secrets of the knowledge of God, and the chooser of His works. 5 If riches are a precious possession in life, what is richer than wisdom, the maker of all things?

8.3.1.en: For she is acquainted with the knowledge of God, and the lover of His works. [4]

8.3.2.en: D. Enjoyment of the knowledge of God, which surpasses the human mind, for He reveals to us the divine mysteries.

8.3.3.en: Since wisdom is a divine hypostasis, "the wisdom of God," she cannot be separated from the Father, for He was never without wisdom. This wisdom, if one may say so, is the storehouses of the divine knowledge and His work and surpassing plan; she reveals the works of God and the surpassing mysteries behind them.

8.4.0.en: If riches are a desirable possession, what is richer than wisdom, which works all things? [5]

8.4.1.en: E. Enjoyment of true riches, not transient temporal possessions, but the love of God and His care and providence that never cease.

8.4.2.en: The wisdom of God is not a static perception or theoretical knowledge, but is ever in motion, the inward movement of love, which also works all things, for she is creator, almighty and governor of all. She is not separated from the divine providence over all creation, heavenly and earthly.

8.5.s.en: 4. Wisdom is at work in her companion

8.5.0.en: 6 And if prudence is that which works, who is more skilled than she in the design of the universe? 7 And if anyone loves righteousness, her labors are the virtues, for she teaches temperance and prudence and justice and fortitude, than which nothing in life is more profitable for men. 8 And if anyone longs for various kinds of knowledge, she knows the things of old and represents the future, and understands the arts of speech and the solving of riddles, and knows signs and wonders before they come to pass, and the events of seasons and times.

8.5.1.en: And if prudence is that which works, who is more skilled than she in the design of beings? [6]

8.5.2.en: F. Enjoyment of understanding and skill. God created man and gave him a mind able to invent, to discover and to progress continually. He is unique among all earthly creatures, always advancing.

8.5.3.en: Our enjoyment of the divine wisdom sanctifies the mind and gives strength and ability to work earnestly, so that man becomes truly skilled in the talents that God has given him.

8.5.4.en: Wisdom is the Creator, the Artist, the Architect of the universe. So when we are united with wisdom we carry the spirit of invention in humility.

8.5.5.en: "The LORD by wisdom hath founded the earth; by understanding hath he established the heavens. By his knowledge the depths are broken up, and the clouds drop down the dew" (Prov 3:19-20).

8.6.0.en: And if a man loves righteousness, her labors are the virtues, for she teaches self-control and prudence and righteousness, and courage, than which nothing in life is more profitable for men. [7]

8.6.1.en: G. Enjoyment of the virtues. At the beginning of the book the wise man linked wisdom with practical righteousness. Now, as the wise man declares the desire of many to be righteous, there is no way to enjoy the righteous, virtuous life except by acquiring divine wisdom.

8.6.2.en: Divine wisdom produces in the children of God four important and principal practical virtues: 1. Contentment. 2. Prudence, or practical understanding. 3. Righteousness.

8.6.3.en: The Lord Christ, the incarnate wisdom, is called the "Sun of righteousness" (Mal 4:2). Whoever He rises upon, He enlightens and gives him surpassing righteousness, while those who do not enjoy His light are deprived of righteousness and live in the darkness of sin.

8.6.4.en: * Those upon whom the "Sun of righteousness" (Mal 4:2), that is, Christ, has not risen, and whose soul's eyes have not been opened and enlightened by the true light, are still under the same darkness of sin and under the same influence of the passions, and they are under the very same punishment, since they have not yet eyes with which to look upon the Father.

8.6.5.en: St. Macarius the Great. 4. Courage or patience:

8.6.6.en: God did not promise His believers who receive heavenly wisdom the broad, easy way and the pampered life, but promised them the narrow way, that they may share with Him His cross and His sufferings, and even His death. The spiritually wise man faces many wars from without as well as from within, but with the multitude of battles he enjoys mighty divine resources by which he overcomes and is crowned.

8.6.7.en: * The man who has truly renounced the world, and cast off the weight of this earth, and thrown off the vain fleshly lusts and the desires for human glory and honors, and has withdrawn from them all with all his heart... and has set firmly in his heart to serve the Lord and worship Him and cleave to Him with his whole being, body and soul, such a man, I say, discovers the presence of the opposition, that is, the hidden passions, and the unseen bonds and the hidden war, that is, the inner battle and struggle, and thus as he entreats the Lord he receives the heavenly armor, the armor of the Holy Spirit, which the blessed Apostle set forth by saying: "the breastplate of righteousness, the helmet of salvation, the shield of faith and the sword of the Spirit" (Eph 6:14). And being armed with these arms he is able to stand against the deceits of the devil even though he is surrounded by evils... he becomes able to war against the principalities of this world. And by his victory over the hostile powers with the help of the Holy Spirit, together with his striving and zeal in every virtue, he becomes prepared for eternal life.

8.6.8.en: St. Macarius the Great. St. Macarius the Great sees that God may delay the answer to prayer and the support of man quickly in his warfare, so that his longing for eternal goods may increase, and that he may train in patience and in striving courageously.

8.6.9.en: * He who does not receive grace quickly because of God's long-suffering burns the more with longing, and grows every day in desire and diligence, and increases in running and striving, and increases in every virtue, and shows hunger and thirst for what is good... and does not turn to contempt and despair and impatience. On the other hand, he does not give himself up to sloth under the guise of pretended patience, saying: "One day or another I shall obtain the grace of God"... but he ought to be more careful and diligent, and not weary or fail, but seek the gift of God, trusting that God is true and cannot lie, for it is He who promised to give His grace to those who seek in faith with all patience to the end.

8.6.10.en: St. Macarius the Great. Perhaps among the most wonderful stories of courage joined with wisdom is the stand of St. John Chrysostom in the year 387 A.D., when the Emperor Theodosius the Great imposed a new additional tax to meet the expense of the celebration of the tenth anniversary of the Emperor Theodosius' reign and the fifth anniversary of his young son Arcadius' sharing power with him.

8.6.11.en: The people of Antioch rose in revolt, for they knew the greed of the tax collectors and the abuse of such a decree, and many fled to the wilderness from the face of the tax collectors. The people took refuge with the governor, who could not intercede for them with the Emperor for fear for his position. They took refuge with the archbishop Flavian (Flavianus), but because of his old age he evaded the situation.

8.6.12.en: Amid popular crowds of every kind, cries soon spread, bringing forth agitation and then revolt. In the twinkling of an eye, without any thought and without any restraint, some went off to smash the statues of the Emperor and the Empress and their son, and threw them into the mud and the filth.

8.6.13.en: All this took place in moments full of the heat of revolt, followed by a calm in which they came to themselves from their drunkenness and felt the hideousness of their crime, and became afraid, expecting their fate and the fate of their city to be severe punishment. The whole city was in confusion, great and small, and no one knew what should be done.

8.6.14.en: The order was issued to burn the whole city, but St. John the priest urged the high priest to travel a distance of more than a thousand kilometers to meet the Emperor and obtain pardon from him, as Moses the prophet did when he interceded before God (Ex 32:32). He asked him not to return without this pardon. Most likely he prepared for him what he should say before the Emperor in a spirit of humility, but with strength and courage. The holy priest stood and said to the people: "Your bishop has set out like a courageous young man who has two wings... I am sure that the mere appearance of the bishop before the pious Emperor will calm the fury of his anger against us, for divine grace shines forth not only from the words of the saint, but in his face also."

8.6.15.en: In a spirit of courage the bishop said to the Emperor: "Your crown, O lord of Rome and the world, is magnificent. It is a proof of your worthiness, but it signifies the generosity of the one who conferred it upon you. But the crown of your humanity owes its merit to your wisdom alone. Men admire the shining precious stones upon your brow, how much more will they admire the victory you win over your heart!" He assured him that if he pardoned the Antiochenes he would gain great glory that the passing of generations would not erase, and he said to him: "Great multitudes will join the Christian religion, saying: Behold the Christian religion, it has quenched the wrath of a man who has no equal in the world."

8.6.16.en: The patriarch, or bishop of Antioch, reached Constantinople, and hastened to the royal court in spite of his great weariness, and met the Emperor and said to him: "I am not a messenger of the people of Antioch, but also an ambassador of God. I have come to you in His name to announce to you: If you forgive men their trespasses and their faults, your heavenly Father will forgive you your trespasses and your faults... Remember that dreadful day when we shall all be bound to give account of our works... All the ambassadors appear before you with the splendor of gold and the multitude of gifts and the abundance of money, but I offer you nothing but the holy law of Jesus Christ, and the example He gave us on the Cross that we might deserve the forgiveness of our sins..."

8.6.17.en: The Emperor's heart was filled with the fear of the Lord when he heard this speech, and he said: "If our Lord and Master Jesus Christ became a servant for our sake, and gave Himself up to the Cross, and asked His Father to forgive those who crucified Him, how then shall I dare to hesitate in forgiving my enemies?"

8.6.18.en: St. Jerome sees that these four virtues which God offers us are the horses that draw the chariot that lifts us up to heaven.

8.6.19.en: * Let these four be the pillars of your horizon, and let them be the four horses that work together to carry you, the chariot of Christ, which runs at its utmost speed to bring you to the goal. There is no necklace more precious than this, nor any jewel more brilliant than this galaxy of stars. They are your adornment, encircling you and protecting you on every side. They are your line of defense and your glory, for every jewel of them is turned into a shield!

8.6.20.en: St. Jerome. In a letter that St. Jerome sent to the senator Pammachius, he mentioned that the members of the household of the one to whom he wrote enjoy these four traits, but while each member enjoys all the traits, each one has a particular trait in which he excels, for he wrote to him: [Each of you possesses the four (virtues), but each has one that is distinctive. You are distinguished by prudence, your mother by righteousness, your virgin sister by endurance (patience), and your wife by contentment. I speak of you as wise, for who can be wiser than he who despises the foolishness of the world and follows Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor 1:24)?]

8.7.0.en: And if anyone desires wide experience, she knows the past and foretells the future, and is skilled in the framing of proverbs and the solving of riddles, and knows signs and wonders before they happen, and the succession of seasons and times. [8]

8.7.1.en: Enjoyment of the Lord Christ lifts man above nature, and carries him to the past, not as a time that has passed and ended but into a life and experience where he finds in his past God's surpassing favors toward him, and his soul rejoices. And he enjoys the present like one at a wedding, in union with the heavenly Bridegroom, and as for the future, it is not unknown to him, for he sees his Christ preparing for him surpassing eternal glories. In other words, he sees in the past a life rejoicing in the Lord and in the future opened heavens.

8.7.2.en: In other words, the Lord Christ adds to man's lifetime a surpassing life, so that the day becomes for him like a thousand years, and he counts every moment of his life as having its own account, since He adds to his mortal temporal life the eternal life of the Lord Christ.

8.7.3.en: Besides these surpassing gifts, the wisdom of God gives him a sanctified mind, so that there are no obscure riddles in his life, but his life becomes a straight and clear way by which he passes into the Father's bosom.

8.7.4.en: In the love of the divine wisdom for us, she hides nothing from us so long as it is for our benefit and edification, so that we perceive surpassing mysteries that spring from the mystery of God's love for us.

8.7.5.en: In brief, the wisdom of God offers us mighty resources to cross the valley of tears while we are in His bosom, finding His cross sweet and experiencing the power of His resurrection, and enjoying heavenly things, as though our heart had ascended with Him and refused to part from Him.

8.8.s.en: 5. A bride who gives glory on earth and in heaven

8.8.0.en: 9 Therefore I determined to take her to me to live with me, knowing that she would be to me a counselor of good things, and a comfort in cares and grief. 10 Because of her I shall have glory among the multitudes, and honor in the presence of the elders, though I am young. 11 And I shall be counted keen in judgment, and shall be admired in the presence of the mighty. 12 When I am silent they will wait for me, and when I speak they will give heed, and when I continue in speaking they will lay their hands upon their mouths. 13 Because of her I shall obtain immortality, and leave behind me an everlasting memory to those who come after me. 14 I shall govern peoples, and nations will be subject to me. 15 Dread monarchs will hear and fear me; among the multitude I shall be seen to be good, and in war courageous. 16 When I enter my house, I shall find rest with her, for there is no bitterness in her company, nor pain in living with her, but gladness and joy.

8.8.1.en: Therefore I determined to take her to be the companion of my life, knowing that she would be to me a counselor of good, and a strengthener in cares and grief. [9]

8.8.2.en: Solomon the wise says: "Wisdom is good with an inheritance: and by it there is profit to them that see the sun" (Eccl 7:11). And also: "When wisdom entereth into thine heart, and knowledge is pleasant unto thy soul; discretion shall preserve thee, understanding shall keep thee" (Prov 2:10-11).

8.8.3.en: He had already spoken of his seeking to take wisdom as a bride, loving her spiritual beauty and rejoicing in union with her (Wis 8:2). Now he speaks of her as the companion of his life, who occupies the seat of command within him, counseling him to good, and supporting and strengthening him in the midst of afflictions and griefs.

8.8.4.en: The wise man says: "woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up" (Eccl 4:10). What then if this second is the Lord Christ, the wisdom of God, dwelling within him, able to raise up even from death, and to grant immortality even if the body is corrupted!

8.9.0.en: So because of her I shall have glory among the multitudes, and honor in the presence of the elders in spite of my youth. [10]

8.9.1.en: Ahasuerus asked Vashti the beautiful queen to appear at a licentious banquet, so that he might boast of her beauty. But the believer boasts of the true beauty, the wisdom of God, fairer than the children of men. The secret of the believer's glory, honor and power is the wisdom of God, which directs his whole inner life.

8.9.2.en: It is said of a Greek king that he said one day: This child rules the world. And when those present were astonished, they asked him: How is this? The king answered: "Greece rules the world, and Athens rules Greece, and I rule Athens, and my wife rules me, and this child rules my wife!" Thus the king points to the hidden power of the family, how such a child has an influence upon the world.

8.9.3.en: If such a child rules the world, how great is the work of the Lord Christ of whom we speak, who is able to direct our whole life!

8.9.4.en: By handing over the steering wheel to wisdom, he enters into a glorious life among the multitudes, so that circumstances, whatever they may be, cannot spoil his inner glory or take away his honor. He bears the marks of the wise elders in spite of his young age.

8.10.0.en: And they will find me keen in the administration of judgment, and will admire me in the presence of the great. [11]

8.10.1.en: Solomon the wise was known for his ability to decide cases with rare wisdom.

8.10.2.en: It is said of the virtuous woman that her husband is known in the gates when he sitteth among the elders of the land (Prov 31:23), judging cases.

8.10.3.en: Thus he who is united with the Lord Christ, the giver of virtue, enjoys the ability to sit among the elders to pass judgments through the grace of his heavenly Bridegroom. And the son of Sirach says: "Many shall commend his understanding; and so long as the world endureth, it shall not be blotted out; his memorial shall not depart away, and his name shall live from generation to generation. Nations shall declare his wisdom, and the congregation shall show forth his praise. If he die, he shall leave a greater name than a thousand: and if he live, he shall increase it" (Sir 39:9-11).

8.11.0.en: And when I am silent they will wait for me, and when I speak they will give heed, and if I continue in speaking, they will lay their hands upon their mouths. [12]

8.11.1.en: When the believer enjoys union with the wisdom of God, his silence, like his words, turns to edification. If the wise man is silent, there is in his silence an eloquent speech that the hearts and minds of those present understand. They do not tire of his silence, but find in his silence blessings that come upon them, and at the same time they await his words as though they were precious jewels worthy of every esteem and honor.

8.11.2.en: The wise man says: "The words of a man's mouth are as deep waters, and the wellspring of wisdom as a flowing brook" (Prov 18:4). If the wise man speaks they listen to him, because the speaker is the Lord working in him, and however much he pours forth words they ask for more. They lay their hands upon their mouths as a sign of their silence in reverence and respect for the speaker (Job 29:9). They do not speak, not out of fear of him, nor because he refuses dialogue, but so that they may use every moment for him to speak.

8.12.0.en: And because of her I shall obtain immortality, and leave behind me to those who come after me an everlasting memory. [13]

8.12.1.en: The wise man had already declared that righteousness is immortal, so whoever acquires wisdom acquires righteousness, and whoever acquires righteousness lives with the Holy One forever. Even before the coming of the Day of Judgment the life of the wise remains a memorial through the generations from which many benefit.

8.12.2.en: * Who dares to refuse to acknowledge that He (the Lord Christ) is immortal, if He Himself makes others immortal? For it is written of the wisdom of God: "Through her I shall obtain immortality" (cf. Wis 8:13). But His immortality according to His nature is one thing, and our immortality is another. There is no comparison between what is perishable and the divine.

8.12.3.en: Divinity alone is the essence that death cannot touch. For this reason the Apostle, although he knows that the human soul and the angels are immortal, declares that God alone has immortality (1 Tim 6:17).

8.13.0.en: St. Ambrose. I shall govern peoples, and nations will be subject to me. [14]

8.13.1.en: The wise man had already declared that God created man to rule the world in holiness and righteousness. By wisdom the believer governs peoples and nations are subject to him, not through civil or military authority, but through the authority of the Spirit, since many desire to follow his example, and his conduct and life become a constitution for them.

8.13.2.en: By wisdom all man's energies and abilities are subjected and work together in marvelous harmony, so that the believer lives like a king with authority over his depths of emotions, thoughts and feelings.

8.14.0.en: Dread kings will hear of me and fear, and I shall appear good among the multitude, and brave in war. [15]

8.14.1.en: Wisdom pours upon us a kind of awe, so that kings and great men fear the righteous wise man, because he is a man of God.

8.14.2.en: The wise man is marked by meekness, so the multitudes love him, and along with meekness he is also marked by courage and patience, so he does not fear the opposition of others against him, but says: "If an army rises against me I will not fear evil."

8.15.0.en: And when I enter my house I shall rest beside her, for there is no bitterness in her company, nor any pain in living with her, but gladness and joy. [16]

8.15.1.en: The dwelling of the Lord Christ in the family gives it gladness and joy. Each member deals with the other members in Christ Jesus, and all compete in giving and bestowing, not in taking and dominating. The family is transformed into a holy church filled with peace and exultation.

8.16.0.en: 17 So when I thought upon these things in myself, and considered in my heart that in kinship with wisdom there is immortality, 18 and in her friendship a good pleasure, and in the labors of her hands unfailing riches, and in the exercise of intimacy with her prudence, and in sharing in her conversation renown, I went about seeking how to take her to myself. 19 Now I was a child of good disposition, and I was given a good soul, 20 or rather, being good, I came into a body undefiled. 21 But when I knew that I could not be chaste unless God gave me chastity, and it was a mark of prudence to know from whom this gift came, I turned to the Lord and besought Him with my whole heart, saying:

8.16.1.en: And after I had thought about these things within myself, and considered in my heart that in being near to wisdom there is immortality. [17]

8.16.2.en: Solomon thought within himself that the nobility of his birth as a son of King David is not what prepares him to obtain wisdom, but she is a divine gift, requiring that he draw near to God in prayer and ask Him to receive her. And by receiving wisdom nothing more occupies him except through his enjoyment of eternity (immortality).

8.16.3.en: By our drawing near to the Lord Christ and entering into fellowship with Him, our heart is lifted up to heaven, and we experience its earnest. We say with the Apostle Paul: "made us sit with him in the heavenly places" (Eph 2:6).

8.16.4.en: "The heart" among the Jews points to the throne of thought and understanding, as we have already pointed out, while the Greeks use the expression "mind Nous" to express thought and understanding.

8.17.0.en: And in her friendship is pure pleasure, and in the labors of her hands unfailing riches, and in the experience of intimacy with her prudence, and in conversing with her a good reputation, I went about seeking how I might take her to myself. [18]

8.17.1.en: When the soul cleaves to the Lord Christ, man enters with Him into a delightful, exalted friendship. He will not suffer from the feeling of isolation, even if all forsake him. It is as though he says with his Savior: "ye shall leave me alone: and yet I am not alone, because the Father is with me."

8.17.2.en: Our cleaving to Him urges us to work and strive, and we count all labor as riches and glory, because we work with Him and by Him and for Him. So our sufferings bear a touch of inward sweetness.

8.17.3.en: Our cleaving to Him pours prudence upon us, so that along with walking in simplicity of heart like little children we carry the wisdom of elders, or as the Lord Christ says: "Be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves," so simplicity is joined with wisdom and understanding.

8.17.4.en: Our cleaving to Him drives us to humility, because He humbled Himself for us, and in His humility He lifted us up and poured upon us surpassing honor.

8.17.5.en: In view of all these gifts, the enjoyment of heavenly things and the delightful friendship and the sweetness amid striving, and wisdom and understanding with simplicity, and the pouring out of inward glory and honor and a good reputation even among the heavenly ones, who would not go about seeking to cleave to Him? Therefore the human soul says of her heavenly Bridegroom, the wisdom of God: "I found him whom my soul loveth: I held him, and would not let him go, until I had brought him into my mother's house, and into the chamber of her that conceived me" (Song 3:4).

8.18.0.en: I was a child of good disposition, and I was given a good soul, [19]

8.18.1.en: The writer returns to the first state of man at his creation, for God created man a good being, "So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them" (Gen 1:27).

8.18.2.en: Here too the writer wishes to affirm that the body in itself is good and undefiled, since through the centuries many philosophies appeared that ascribe corruption to the body by its nature. For this reason the Fathers of the Church often affirm that the corruption of man springs from the corruption of his will and not from the nature of the body.

8.19.0.en: But rather, being good, I came into a body undefiled. [20]

8.19.1.en: The writer does not mean here that the human soul has a pre-existence, and because it is good it received an undefiled body, but we understand it through the book as a whole: he wishes to affirm the leading role of the soul even over the body. The subject of original sin was not in the writer's mind at all.

8.19.2.en: Origen sees that the speaker here is Jesus Christ, who alone was in the womb of His mother with a body not from the seed of men, and bore in Himself no corruption of Adam.

8.20.0.en: And when I knew that I could not be wise unless God gave her to me - and it was part of wisdom to know from whom this grace comes - I prayed to the Lord and besought Him, and said with my whole heart: [21]

8.20.1.en: The wise man spoke of his longing for wisdom and asked it of God, realizing that he could not enjoy her unless she were given to him by God. What he said here applies to every sincere and true virtue, because virtue is nothing but the enjoyment of fellowship with the Righteous Holy One.

8.20.2.en: This is what St. Augustine expressed in his Confessions when he spoke of chastity in the same spirit.

8.20.3.en: In a wonderful prayer St. Augustine speaks to God with the certainty that however difficult His commandments may seem, they are within reach of our hand, so long as God grants us to carry them out.

8.20.4.en: * All my hope is in Thy great and surpassing mercies. Give what Thou commandest, and command what Thou wilt. Thou dost impose chastity upon us. One says: "And when I knew that I could not obtain her except God gave her... this is wisdom, to know from whom this grace comes.

8.20.5.en: * You seek wisdom, my son, that you may be steadfast in this race, for you entered upon it from the beginning under the influence of wisdom. Let it be part of your wisdom to know from whom this grace (gift) comes. "Commit thy way unto the LORD; trust also in him; and he shall bring it to pass. And he shall bring forth thy righteousness as the light, and thy judgment as the noonday" (Ps 37:5-6).

8.20.6.en: * As for chastity, I thought it was within my power (though I did not find this power in me). I was foolish, for I did not know what is written: "No one can be chaste unless Thou give it," and that Thou wilt give it to me if I knock with my inward sighs at the door of Thine ears, and with right faith fix my attention upon Thee.

8.20.7.en: * Without doubt the value of the gift of chastity was known to the one who said: "I knew that no one can be chaste unless God give (this) gift." So he not only knew the greatness of the benefit of chastity, and how it must be longed for and desired, but that unless God gives it it cannot exist. Wisdom taught him this.

8.20.8.en: * He says: "And when I knew that no one can be chaste unless God give (chastity), and this is part of wisdom, to know from whom this gift (grace) comes" (Wis 8:21). These two gifts, wisdom and chastity, are great. Truly by wisdom we are formed according to the knowledge of God, and by chastity we are not conformed to this world.

8.20.9.en: * When He commands us, saying: "Go not after your lusts" (Sir 18:30), let us say to Him: "We know that no man can be chaste unless God give it to him" (cf. Wis 8:21); what do we say but: Give what Thou hast commanded.

8.20.10.en: * No one can be chaste unless God grants him this gift, nor is the love of God shed abroad in our hearts from ourselves, but by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us (Rom 5:5).

8.20.11.en: * Wisdom and chastity are the two gifts of God, that is, they are not from others.

8.20.12.en: * Certainly such commandments could not have been given if man did not have freedom of will, by which he obeys the divine commandments, for it is necessary for keeping the commandments of chastity. For this reason it is said in the Book of Wisdom: "I knew that no one can be chaste unless God give it to him - and it was part of wisdom to know from whom this grace comes" (cf. Wis 8:21).

8.20.13.en: * If even in the body, the least element of its nature, all the lofty things, such as beauty and vitality and health and so on, are the work of God, how much more are the lofty things that belong to the soul.

8.20.14.en: * It is a very great matter that we aim to speak of what He (God) gives, for in the first place we say and affirm that chastity is a gift from God (Wis 8:21). It is written in the Book of Wisdom that no one can be chaste unless God grants him this.

8.20.16.en: May my soul be joined to You,
